cards.question: Why must CHIP-8 ROM files be loaded at memory address 0x200 (512 decimal) instead of 0x000?
cards.answer: Memory from 0x000 to 0x1FF is reserved for the built-in hexadecimal fontset and interpreter memory; program execution begins at 0x200.

cards.question: What is the maximum allowed file size for a CHIP-8 ROM in standard 4KB RAM systems?
cards.answer: 3,584 bytes (4096 - 512 = 3584), since total addressable memory is 4,096 bytes and the first 512 bytes are reserved.

cards.question: How are 16-bit CHIP-8 opcodes fetched from the byte-oriented memory array?
cards.answer: By combining two successive big-endian bytes from memory at PC using bitwise shift and OR: uint16_t opcode = (memory[PC] << 8) | memory[PC + 1];.

cards.question: How does the addition instruction 7XNN differ from 8XY4 regarding the VF flag register?
cards.answer: 7XNN adds an immediate value to VX without modifying VF on overflow, whereas 8XY4 adds VY to VX and sets VF = 1 if the sum exceeds 255 (carry) and 0 otherwise.

cards.question: How does the borrow/carry flag VF work for the subtraction instruction 8XY5 (VX = VX - VY)?
cards.answer: VF is set to 1 if there is no borrow (VX >= VY), and set to 0 if a borrow occurs (VX < VY).

cards.question: How does the DXYN display instruction handle screen rendering and collision detection?
cards.answer: It draws an N-byte tall sprite using bitwise XOR on the 64x32 monochrome display, setting VF = 1 if any lit pixel is toggled off (collision) and 0 otherwise.

cards.question: How do coordinate wrapping and sprite clipping differ in the DXYN instruction?
cards.answer: The starting (X, Y) coordinate wraps around the screen using modulo (X % 64, Y % 32), but sprite pixels extending past the right or bottom edges are clipped rather than wrapped.
